title: Every legal move named, and the one-stroke rule proved
summary: Finish linear equations with fractions, decimals and letters on both sides, naming every move out loud, then prove why a drawing with more than two odd corners can never be traced in one stroke.
materials: the field journal, open at the sprint's proof pages
jumbo sidewalk chalk, for the ladder and the envelope on the driveway
ten coins for the monster's circle

problems.prompt: A drum loop is 8 beats long and repeats with no gap. The singer comes in on beat 100. Counting from the start of the loop it lands in, which beat of that loop is it?
explanation: Clock math: divide and keep the leftover, because the loop starts over every 8 beats.
Twelve whole loops fill 96 beats, and 100 sits past that.
So the singer lands on the fourth beat of the thirteenth loop.
problems.useAgain: when a pattern repeats in blocks and you need what lands on a beat too far away to count to.
hints: Work out how many beats one whole loop takes before you look at 100.
Divide 100 by the loop length and watch the leftover, not the number of whole loops.
problems.socraticHint: Which beats before 100 sound exactly like beat 100 does?

variant.prompt: The loop is now 6 beats long and still repeats with no gap. The singer comes in on beat 95. Which beat of its loop is that?

problems.prompt: A metronome sits at 144 beats a minute. You halve it, halve it again, then halve it once more. Where does it land?
explanation: Three halvings in a row is one division by 2 times 2 times 2, which is 8.
So the setting lands at 144 divided by 8.
144, 72, 36, and one halving still to go. Stopping early lands on 36, which is the trap.
problems.useAgain: when a number is halved or doubled the same way several times over.
hints: Do not divide by 6. Halving three times is not the same as dividing by 6.
Write the settings in a row, starting at 144, and halve as you go along the row.
problems.socraticHint: How many 2s are standing in the line when you halve three times?

variant.prompt: A metronome sits at 200 beats a minute and you halve it three times. Where does it land?

problems.prompt: A click track puts its first click on beat 1, and after that a click lands every 4 beats. A click lands on beat 41. Which click is it, counting the first one as click 1?
explanation: Count the gaps, not the clicks. Every click after the first sits 4 beats along.
From beat 1 to beat 41 is 40 beats, and 40 divided by 4 is 10 gaps.
Ten gaps come after the first click, so the click on beat 41 is one further on than ten.
problems.useAgain: when things sit evenly along a line and you have to number one of them.
hints: Count the gaps between clicks first, not the clicks themselves.
How many beats lie between beat 1 and beat 41, and how big is a single gap?
problems.socraticHint: If the first click sat on beat 0 instead of beat 1, would your count change?

variant.prompt: The click track puts its first click on beat 2, and a click lands every 3 beats after that. A click lands on beat 35. Which click is it, counting the first one as click 1?

problems.prompt: Two drummers start together on beat 1. After that one hits every 4 beats and the other every 6. Which is the first beat where they hit together again?
explanation: Both leave beat 1 together, so ask how far each one travels before they meet.
One travels in fours, the other in sixes, and the first shared distance is 12 beats.
Twelve beats past beat 1 lands on beat 13. Answering 12 forgets that the counting began on beat 1, not beat 0.
problems.useAgain: when two things repeat on different beats and you need the first beat they share.
hints: The starting beat is not beat 0, so the meeting beat is not just the shared distance.
Find the first number that both fours and sixes reach, then walk that far from the start.
problems.socraticHint: What would the answer have been if both drummers had started on beat 0 instead?

variant.prompt: Two drummers start together on beat 1, then one hits every 6 beats and the other every 9. Which is the first beat where they hit together again?

problems.prompt: A track runs at 120 beats a minute and lasts 3 minutes and 20 seconds. How many beats is that?
explanation: At 120 beats a minute the drum lands twice in every second.
Three minutes and 20 seconds is 200 seconds.
Two beats in each of those 200 seconds gives the total.
problems.useAgain: when a rate is given per minute and the time you are handed is not in minutes.
hints: Turn the length into seconds before you touch the beat rate.
How many beats land in a single second at this rate?
problems.socraticHint: Which unit are you counting in, and does the rate you were given agree with it?

variant.prompt: A track runs at 100 beats a minute and lasts 2 minutes and 30 seconds. How many beats is that?

problem.prompt: Jumbo chalk on the driveway makes a grid 4 squares across and 3 squares up. Using only the chalk lines, how many rectangles of any size can be outlined on it?
explanation: A rectangle is fixed the moment you choose its two side lines and its two end lines.
The grid has 5 lines running up and down, and there are 10 ways to pick two of them.
It has 4 lines running across, and there are 6 ways to pick two of those.
Any pair of up-and-down lines works with any pair of across lines, so the two counts multiply.
Counting only the squares gives a far smaller number, because most rectangles here are not square.
problem.useAgain: when a shape is pinned down by two separate choices, so the counts multiply.
hints: Do not hunt rectangles one at a time. Ask what two decisions fix one rectangle.
Count the lines running up and down, then count the ways two of them can be picked.
problem.socraticHint: How many chalk lines does the pencil have to touch to close one rectangle, and in which directions?

figure.alt: A chalk grid 4 squares across and 3 squares up, made of 5 lines running up and down crossed by 4 lines running across.

variant.prompt: Same chalk, a smaller grid: 3 squares across and 3 squares up. How many rectangles of any size can be outlined on it?

steps.title: Linear equations, the end-game: fractions, decimals and letters on both sides

problems.prompt: A gear-rental log at the trailhead office shows two facts: 2 day passes and 3 week passes cost $31 altogether, and 5 day passes and 3 week passes cost $46 altogether. The week-pass price was the same both times. What does one day pass cost?
explanation: Both facts have exactly 3 week passes in them, so subtracting one fact from the other cancels the week passes completely.
5 day passes minus 2 day passes is 3 day passes, and 46 dollars minus 31 dollars is 15 dollars.
3 day passes cost 15 dollars, so one day pass costs 5 dollars.
Check: 2 day passes at 5 dollars is 10 dollars.
So the week passes cost 31 minus 10, which is 21 dollars for 3, or 7 dollars each.
In the second fact, 5 times 5 plus 3 times 7 is 25 plus 21, which is 46.
problems.useAgain: when two facts share the exact same amount of one unknown, so subtracting one fact from the other cancels it.
hints: Look for a part that is identical in both facts. Subtracting the facts should make that part disappear.
Once one unknown cancels, the difference between the two facts is a plain equation in the other unknown.
problems.socraticHint: If both facts had the exact same number of week passes, what would subtracting one fact from the other actually be counting?

variant.prompt: A different log shows: 2 day passes and 4 week passes cost $32, and 6 day passes and 4 week passes cost $48. What does one day pass cost?

problems.prompt: Here are four legal moves that solve 7 - 2n = 4n - 11. More than one order is legal, so use this one: letters first, then the loose numbers, then the divide, then read it off. Each move is used once.
explanation: Add 2n to both sides first, so the letters gather on one side: 7 = 6n - 11.
Add 11 to both sides, which clears the loose number sitting with the letters: 18 = 6n.
Divide both sides by 6 to leave one n on its own, then read the answer off.
Adding 11 before the 2n is also legal and lands on the same n, so the question named the order it wants.
Dividing first is legal as well, but it leaves sixths on both sides and more work.
problems.useAgain: when you can nearly see the answer but need the moves that get there written down.
hints: Two of these four could go either way round, which is why the question named an order.
Which single move puts every n on the same side of the equals sign?
problems.socraticHint: The question named an order, so what makes one of these moves a bad one to do first?

variant.prompt: Four legal moves solve 9 - 3k = 6k - 9. Put them in the same order: letters, loose numbers, divide, read it off.

problems.prompt: Solve for x: x/3 + x/4 = 7.
explanation: Thirds and quarters both fit into twelfths, so multiply every term on both sides by 12.
That turns the equation into 4x + 3x = 84, with no fractions left anywhere.
So 7x = 84, and dividing both sides by 7 finishes it.
Multiplying only the left side would tip the balance and change the answer.
problems.useAgain: when fractions clutter an equation and you would rather work in whole numbers.
hints: Find one number that both bottoms divide into.
Multiply every single term by that number, including the one on the right of the equals sign.
problems.socraticHint: What happens to a fraction when you multiply it by a number its bottom divides into?

variant.prompt: Solve for x: x/2 + x/5 = 7.

problems.prompt: A bake-sale record from the trailhead stand: 2 brownies and 3 cookies sold for $13. 3 brownies and 2 cookies sold for $12. What does one brownie cost?
explanation: Neither fact shares a matching count of brownies or cookies, so cancelling needs scaling first.
Scale the first fact by 3 and the second fact by 2.
That gives 6 brownies plus 9 cookies equals 39, and 6 brownies plus 4 cookies equals 24.
Now both facts share 6 brownies, so subtracting cancels them: 5 cookies cost 39 minus 24, which is 15 dollars.
One cookie is 3 dollars.
Put that back into the first real fact: 2 brownies plus 9 dollars is 13, so one brownie is 2 dollars.
problems.useAgain: when neither unknown has a matching count in the two facts, so one or both facts need scaling before anything cancels.
hints: Neither unknown cancels as the facts stand. Find a number to scale each fact by so that one of them will.
Scale both facts up until one unknown has the exact same count in both, then subtract.
problems.socraticHint: Which small whole number do the brownie counts in the two facts both divide into evenly, and what would scaling both facts up to reach it do?

variant.prompt: A second bake-sale record: 2 brownies and 3 cookies sold for $18. 3 brownies and 2 cookies sold for $17. What does one brownie cost?

problems.prompt:
Priya solved 4(x - 3) = 2(x + 5) like this:
Line 1: Multiply out the brackets: 4x - 3 = 2x + 10.
Line 2: Take 2x off both sides: 2x - 3 = 10.
Line 3: Add 3 to both sides: 2x = 13.
Line 4: Divide both sides by 2: x = 6.5.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 1 is wrong: the 4 has to multiply every term inside its bracket, not just the x. It should read 4x minus 12, not 4x minus 3.
Lines 2 through 4 are each done correctly. They just build correctly on the wrong equation Line 1 handed them.
Starting from the true expansion, 4x - 12 = 2x + 10, taking 2x off both sides gives 2x - 12 = 10.
Then adding 12 gives 2x = 22.
Dividing by 2 gives x equals 11, not 6.5.
A number stuck to a letter outside a bracket has a job at every single term inside it.
problems.useAgain: when a number outside a bracket has more than one term to multiply inside it.
hints: Every arithmetic move after the brackets come off is done correctly. Look at the moment the brackets actually open.
A number outside a bracket has a job at every single term inside, not just the first one it touches.
problems.socraticHint: How many terms live inside that bracket, and did every single one of them get multiplied?

variant.prompt:
Priya solved 5(y - 3) = 2(y - 6) like this:
Line 1: Multiply out the brackets: 5y - 15 = 2y + 12.
Line 2: Take 2y off both sides: 3y - 15 = 12.
Line 3: Add 15 to both sides: 3y = 27.
Line 4: Divide both sides by 3: y = 9.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Two skate parks. The first charges $12 to join and then $3 for every visit. The second charges nothing to join and $5 for every visit. After how many visits do the two cost the same?
explanation: Name the unknown first: let v stand for the number of visits.
The first park costs 12 + 3v dollars, and the second costs 5v dollars.
Same cost means 12 + 3v = 5v. Take 3v off both sides and 12 = 2v.
Below that number of visits the second park is cheaper, and above it the first one is.
problems.useAgain: when two prices have different joining fees and different rates, and you want the visit where they cross.
hints: Write each park's cost as one expression before you compare anything.
What has to be true of the two expressions at the visit where they match?
problems.socraticHint: Which park is cheaper on visit one, and does it stay cheaper forever?

variant.prompt: The first park charges $20 to join and then $2 a visit. The second charges nothing to join and $6 a visit. After how many visits do they cost the same?

problems.prompt: How many numbers make 2(3x - 5) = 6x - 10 true?
explanation: Open the bracket on the left and it says 6x - 10, which is what the right side already said.
Every legal move from there leaves both sides identical, ending at 0 = 0.
An equation true for every number is not broken. It is an identity.
Compare 2(3x - 5) = 6x - 9, where the same moves leave -10 = -9, which no x can fix.
problems.useAgain: when the letters vanish from both sides and you have to say what that means.
hints: Open the bracket before you decide anything.
What is left standing after every x has cancelled out?
problems.socraticHint: If the letters disappear, what is the equation still telling you about the two numbers left behind?

variant.prompt: How many numbers make 4(2x + 3) = 8x + 7 true?

steps.title: The distance that is really a triangle, and picking teams two ways

problems.prompt: Point A is at (1, 1) and point B is at (4, 5). What is the distance from A to B?
explanation: The straight-line distance is the longest side of a right triangle built from the across and the up.
Across is 4 minus 1, which is 3. Up is 5 minus 1, which is 4.
3 squared plus 4 squared is 9 plus 16, which is 25, and its square root is 5.
problems.useAgain: when the straight-line distance between two plotted points is needed, using the difference in x and the difference in y as the two legs.
hints: Find how far apart the two points are across, and how far apart they are up.
Square both of those differences, add them, then take the square root.
problems.socraticHint: If you drew a horizontal line and a vertical line to connect these two points with a right angle, what would the two straight sides measure?

variant.prompt: Point A is at (2, 2) and point B is at (10, 8). What is the distance from A to B?

problems.prompt: Point A is at (0, 0) and point B is at (9, 12). What is the distance from A to B?
explanation: Across is 9, and up is 12.
9 squared plus 12 squared is 81 plus 144, which is 225, and its square root is 15.
problems.useAgain: when both points involve bigger numbers, so the two-leg right triangle idea still applies exactly the same way.
hints: Find the across distance and the up distance between the two points.
Square both, add them, then take the square root.
problems.socraticHint: Does it matter for this method whether one of the points sits at the origin?

variant.prompt: Point A is at (0, 0) and point B is at (8, 15). What is the distance from A to B?

problems.prompt: A group of 5 friends wants to send exactly 3 of them to represent the class. How many different 3-person teams are possible, where order does not matter?
explanation: Sending Ann, Bo and Cy is the same team no matter what order they were picked in.
Counting every different group of 3 out of the 5 friends, without counting the same team twice in a different order, gives 10 teams.
problems.useAgain: when a fixed-size team or group is chosen from a bigger set, and the picking order does not change who ends up on the team.
hints: Would picking the same 3 people in a different order make a different team?
Count every different group of 3 people from the 5, without repeats.
problems.socraticHint: Once the team is picked, does anyone remember or care in what order they were chosen?

variant.prompt: A group of 6 friends wants to send exactly 3 of them to represent the class. How many different 3-person teams are possible, where order does not matter?

problems.prompt: How many different 2-person pairs can be made from a group of 6 people, where order does not matter, so Ann-and-Bo is the same pair as Bo-and-Ann?
explanation: Since a pair does not care which person was named first, Ann-and-Bo counts only once.
Counting every different unordered pair from the 6 people gives 15 pairs.
problems.useAgain: when pairs are counted from a group and naming the two people in a different order should not create a new pair.
hints: Is Ann-and-Bo a different pair from Bo-and-Ann?
Count every different unordered pair from the 6 people.
problems.socraticHint: If you listed every ordered pair and then noticed each unordered pair was counted twice, how would you fix the total?

variant.prompt: How many different 2-person pairs can be made from a group of 7 people, where order does not matter?

figure.alt: White to move. A white bishop on a3 faces the black king on e3 with a black queen on g5 behind it on the same diagonal.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move forces the king to move and wins the queen behind it?
explanation: Black's king on e3 and queen on g5 share the same diagonal.
Bc1 checks the king first, so it must step off that diagonal.
Once the king moves, the queen behind it is exposed on the same line.
problems.useAgain: when a check lines up with a bigger prize sitting further along the same diagonal.
hints: Which diagonal already holds both the black king and the black queen?
Move your bishop onto that diagonal so it checks the king first.
problems.socraticHint: After the king moves out of check, what is still sitting on that diagonal?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move forces the king to move and wins the rook behind it?

figure.alt: White to move. A white bishop on c6 faces the black king on d3 with a black rook on b1 behind it on the same diagonal.
White to move. A white knight on d4 can capture a black pawn on f5, forking a black queen on d6 and a black rook on h6.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move captures a pawn and attacks two pieces at once?
explanation: Nxf5 takes a free pawn and lands on a square that attacks both d6 and h6.
Black's queen and rook sit on exactly those two squares, with nothing defending them.
White wins a pawn now and more material next move.
problems.useAgain: when a capture also lands your piece on a square that forks two others.
hints: Before you capture, check what the knight would attack from its new square.
Look at both of the two squares it would attack from there.
problems.socraticHint: Besides the free pawn, what else does the knight land on top of?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move captures a pawn and attacks two pieces at once?

figure.alt: White to move. A white knight on e3 can capture a black pawn on d5, forking a black rook on c7 and a black queen on f6.
White to move. Black's king on h8 is boxed in by its own rook on g8 and pawns on g7 and h7, with a white knight on h6.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?
explanation: Black's own rook on g8 and pawns on g7 and h7 block every escape square around its king.
Nf7 checks the king with nothing left to run to and nothing that can capture the knight.
This is a smothered mate: black's own pieces trap its king.
problems.useAgain: when a king's own pieces block every escape square and a knight can still reach it.
hints: Look at what surrounds the black king. Whose pieces are boxing it in?
Find the knight move that checks the king from a square nothing can reach.
problems.socraticHint: If black's own rook were not sitting there, could the king escape that way?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?

figure.alt: White to move. Black's king on a8 is boxed in by its own rook on b8 and pawns on a7 and b7, with a white knight on a6.
White to move. A white bishop on g2 faces a black queen alone on d5.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move wins the undefended black queen?
explanation: Black's queen sits alone on d5 with no defender.
The white bishop already shares that diagonal.
Bxd5 wins the queen for a bishop, the biggest trade on the board.
problems.useAgain: when the biggest piece on the board has nobody watching its back.
hints: Which black piece is worth the most, and does anything defend it?
Which white piece already shares a line with it?
problems.socraticHint: Out of everything you could capture, which one wins the most material?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move wins the undefended black queen?

steps.title: The one-stroke rule proved, two peaks, and the month's monster in small cases

problems.prompt: Konigsberg had four pieces of land joined by seven bridges. The island carried 5 bridges and the other three pieces carried 3 each. A walk that crosses every bridge exactly once is possible. True or false?
explanation: Call a piece of land odd when an odd number of bridges meet it. All four pieces here are odd.
The one-stroke rule: a drawing can be traced without lifting the pencil only when it has no odd corners, or exactly two.
Four odd corners is more than two, so no such walk exists anywhere in that town.
Nothing here depends on the total of seven bridges. Only the odd count decides it.
problems.useAgain: when you are asked whether a drawing or a route can be done in one unbroken stroke.
hints: Count the bridges meeting each piece of land before you try any route at all.
Sort the four pieces into two piles: even numbers of bridges and odd numbers of bridges.
problems.socraticHint: You have to arrive at a piece of land and leave it again. What does that do to its bridges, two at a time?

variant.prompt: A different town also has four pieces of land, and you can already get from any piece to any other. They carry 2, 2, 4 and 4 bridges. A walk that crosses every bridge exactly once is possible. True or false?

problems.prompt: The envelope figure: a rectangle with both of its diagonals drawn in, and a triangular roof on the top edge whose peak joins the two top corners. How many of its corners have an odd number of lines meeting them?
explanation: Count the lines meeting each corner, one corner at a time.
Each bottom corner has the bottom edge, a side edge and one diagonal: three lines.
Each top corner has a side edge, the top edge, a diagonal and a roof line: four lines. The peak has two.
The two diagonals cross in the middle, and four lines meet there, which is even. So the odd corners are the bottom pair.
problems.useAgain: when a figure has to be checked for tracing before a pencil stroke is wasted on it.
hints: Five corners, not four. The roof peak is a corner too.
Put a dot on one corner and count only the lines that actually touch that dot.
problems.socraticHint: The two diagonals cross in the middle. Does counting that crossing as a corner change your answer?

figure.alt: An envelope shape: a rectangle with both diagonals drawn corner to corner, and a triangular roof on the top edge whose peak joins the two top corners.

variant.prompt: Now rub out the roof, leaving just the rectangle and its two diagonals. How many corners have an odd number of lines meeting them?

problems.prompt: Write the proof to the rubric: why can a drawing with more than two odd corners never be traced in one unbroken stroke? Use the doors argument, and say what the start and the end are allowed to do that the middle corners are not.

mustMention: passing through a corner uses two lines, one in and one out
a corner in the middle of the walk spends its lines in pairs, so its count is even
only the start corner and the end corner are allowed to be odd
three odd corners would need three ends, and a stroke has only two

explanation: Think of every line at a corner as a door. Arriving spends one door, leaving spends another.
A corner you only pass through therefore spends its doors two at a time, so its count stays even.
The start corner spends one extra door leaving at the beginning, and the end corner one extra arriving.
So an odd corner has to be the start or the end. A single stroke has one of each and no more.
Three odd corners would need a third end, and no such thing exists. That is where the limit of two comes from.
problems.useAgain: when you have to show something is impossible rather than just failing to find it.
hints: Do not argue about any particular drawing. Argue about what one corner has to do.
Picture a corner the pencil visits in the middle of the stroke, and count the doors that visit spends.
problems.socraticHint: What is true of the very first corner and the very last one that is not true of any other corner?

problems.prompt: Chalk a ladder on the driveway: two long lines with four rungs joining them, making three squares in a row. What does the one-stroke rule say about tracing it?
options: 4 odd corners, so it cannot be traced
2 odd corners, so it can be traced
0 odd corners, so it can be traced
8 odd corners, so it cannot be traced
explanation: The ladder has eight corners, four on each long line.
The four corners at the two ends have two lines each: one rung and one stretch of long line.
The four in the middle have three each, because the long line runs away from them in both directions.
That is four odd corners, which is more than two, so no unbroken stroke exists.
problems.useAgain: when a real drawing has to be checked before anyone starts walking it.
hints: Count the corners first. There are more of them than the squares suggest.
A corner where a rung meets the middle of a long line has how many lines at it?
problems.socraticHint: Which corners of the ladder are different from the others, and what makes them different?

variant.prompt: Rub out one end square, leaving a ladder of two squares in a row. What does the rule say now?
options: 0 odd corners, so it can be traced
2 odd corners, so it can be traced
4 odd corners, so it cannot be traced
3 odd corners, so it cannot be traced

problems.prompt: An AMC 8 style peak, untimed, and you explain it back afterwards. A bag holds 5 white stones and 6 black stones. A move pulls out two stones: if they match, one black stone goes back in; if they differ, one white stone goes back in. Every move leaves one fewer stone, so one stone is left at the end. That last stone is white. True or false?
explanation: Do not chase the moves. Watch the white stones and count them after each kind of move.
Two whites out, a black in: the white count drops by two.
Two blacks out, a black in: the white count does not move.
One of each out, a white in: the white goes out and a white comes back, so the count holds.
Every move changes the white count by two or not at all, so odd stays odd. It starts at five, an odd number.
An odd count can never be zero, so a white stone is still there at the end.
problems.useAgain: when every move in a puzzle leaves one count odd or even exactly as it found it.
hints: Do not hunt for a sequence of moves. Hunt for something no move can change.
Count the white stones after each of the three kinds of move and see what survives.
problems.socraticHint: The black stones change a lot. Is there anything about the white ones that no move is allowed to touch?

variant.prompt: Same bag and same rule, but it starts with 4 white stones and 7 black. That last stone is white. True or false?

problems.prompt: An AMC 8 style peak, untimed, and you explain it back afterwards. A yard holds only chickens and cows. There are 20 heads and 56 legs altogether. How many cows are in the yard?
explanation: Name the unknowns: c chickens and w cows. One head each, so c + w = 20.
The legs give a second sentence: 2c + 4w = 56.
From the first sentence c is 20 - w. Put that in: 40 - 2w + 4w = 56.
That tidies to 40 + 2w = 56, so 2w = 16 and w is half of 16.
problems.useAgain: when a story hands you two facts about two unknown counts.
hints: Two unknowns need two sentences. What are the two facts the yard gives you?
Write one unknown in terms of the other, and then only one letter is left to solve for.
problems.socraticHint: If every animal in the yard were a chicken, how many legs would be missing?

variant.prompt: The same yard, still only chickens and cows. This time there are 30 heads and 84 legs. How many cows?

problems.prompt: The month's monster, in small cases. Six coins stand in a circle, numbered 1 to 6 around it. Counting starts at coin 1: coin 1 stays, coin 2 is taken away, coin 3 stays, coin 4 is taken away, and the counting keeps going round, always removing every second coin still standing. Which coin is the last one left?
explanation: Lay six coins out and take them away for real. Guessing this is slower than doing it.
First time round, coins 2, 4 and 6 go, so coins 1, 3 and 5 are still standing.
The count carries straight on from coin 6 to coin 1, which stays, so coin 3 goes next.
Then coin 5 stays and coin 1 goes, leaving coin 5 alone in the circle.
Write this case into the monster's table and leave the pattern alone for now. The pattern is the monster.
problems.useAgain: when a rule keeps running around a loop and only acting it out will tell you the end.
hints: Use real coins in a real circle. Your fingers will not lose track the way your head will.
After the first time round, do not start counting again at coin 1. Carry on from where you stopped.
problems.socraticHint: When you have been all the way round once, whose turn is it next, and why is that the part people get wrong?

variant.prompt: Nine coins in a circle now, same rule, counting starting at coin 1. Which coin is the last one left?

problems.prompt: A drawing has exactly two odd corners, so the rule says it can be traced in one stroke. Where must the pencil start?
options: At either of the two odd corners
It cannot be traced at all
explanation: An odd corner spends its lines in pairs except for one line left over.
That leftover line has to be the very first line drawn or the very last one.
So each odd corner must be an end of the stroke, and a stroke has exactly two ends.
Starting anywhere else leaves an odd corner with nowhere to put its leftover line.
problems.useAgain: when a figure passes the rule and you still have to decide where to put the pencil down.
hints: The rule tells you more than yes or no. It also tells you where the ends have to go.
Think about the leftover line at an odd corner, and when in the stroke it could be drawn.
problems.socraticHint: If a drawing had no odd corners at all, where would the stroke have to start and finish?

variant.prompt: A different drawing has no odd corners at all. Where must the pencil start?
options: It cannot be traced at all
Anywhere, and it comes back to where it started

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Copy 0.4y + 1.2 = 0.9y - 0.5 into the field journal. Under it write every line of your solution, and beside every line name the move that produced it in your own words: what you did, to which side, and why it was legal. Then write one last sentence saying what a chant would have hidden from you here.

steps.title: Explain it out loud
steps.prompt: Record yourself explaining, without drawing anything, why the chalk ladder of three squares cannot be traced in one stroke while the ladder of two squares can. Say what you counted, what the count told you, and what single line you could add to the three-square ladder to make it traceable.
